newsitem.title: ITALY: Anglican leader says AIDS victims need compassion.
newsitem.headline: Anglican leader says AIDS victims need compassion.

text.p: The Archbishop of Canterbury, George Carey, on Tuesday criticised people who say AIDS sufferers are dying because they sinned.
"No-one is beyond its reach. Good and bad, moral and immoral, rich and especially poor, young and old are caught in its grip," the Anglican leader said in a sermon at an Episcopal chruch in Rome.
Carey, the spiritual head of the 70 million-member worldwide Anglican Communion, is in Rome for a three-day official visit to Pope John Paul at the Vatican.
Carey recalled that several years ago he had been criticised by some people for being a sponsor of World Aids Day, which was marked again last Sunday.
"'You can't possibly lend your name to help people who are only dying because they have sinned,'" he quoted his critics as saying at the time.
"I happen to think compassion for sinners is a Christian calling...many people with AIDS are not responsible themselves for contracting the disease," Carey said.
"We are all recipients of God's judgment and love together. What AIDS victims require from us is not condemnation but compassion; not accusation but affirmation; not mockery but mercy," Carey said.
The Pope has called on all Catholics to be compassionate to AIDS sufferers but he is opposed to the use of condoms to guard against the disease.
The Roman Catholic Church teaches that chastity and keeping sex within heterosexual marriage is the only acceptable way of fighting the spread of the disease.
The Vatican's semi-official newspaper on Monday criticised organisers of World AIDS Day events in Italy for handing out condoms.
L'Osservatore Romano said they had transformed World AIDS Day on Sunday "into a series of vulgar appeals for the use of condoms".
A recent U.N. report said that more than three million people, mostly under 25 years of age, have become infected with the AIDS virus in 1996.

The new cases bring to nearly 23 million the total number who are infected. Since AIDS was discovered over 15 years ago, 6.4 million people, including 1.4 million children, have died, with 1.5 million succumbing to the disease in 1996.
Africa is the worst hit, with 14 million people or 63 percent of the total.
